Course Approval Process

The Course/Program Approval Process at URI 1.
Initial Submission on Kuali.
Faculty members submit course (for both new and modified classes) and program proposals within Kuali Curriculum Management.
Kuali provides workflow at URI for curricular changes and is in the university’s Microsoft 365 suite; further information and login link can be found here: https://web.uri.edu/facsen/kuali/.
A library impact statement will be generated for new courses within one week of submission to Kuali.
Crosslisted classes, courses/programs that might overlap with existing offerings, and classes/programs assuming prerequisites from other departments need to provide documentation regarding approval from those other relevant academic units.
New programs need to allow two weeks for a Budget Impact Statement to be completed by the Budget Office.
Note: new programs must also complete the New Program Assessment Plan (https://web.uri.edu/atl/assessment/newprograms/) and submit it to the Assessment Team at assess@uri.edu. 2.
Approval Requirements.

Once a faculty member submits a new course proposal, either the department’s curriculum committee or the department chair/program head must approve it based on the governance structure of the department.
This approval requires a vote of the faculty of the originating department.
Courses not originating within a specific department or college must be approved by the governing committee responsible for administering the program.
As part of their approval, the departmental curriculum committee or chairs/program heads must submit an official statement confirming departmental approval via faculty vote for the proposal. 3.
College-level Review.
After approval by the department, the proposal is reviewed for approval by the college curriculum committee(s), and then approved by the college dean or delegate.
Colleges assess course proposals for issues such as staffing, intra-college departmental and interdepartmental overlap, and collegewide programmatic needs and requirements. 4.
Senate Committee Review.
After college-level approval, proposals go to the Faculty Senate Specialist who formats and prepares them for the following month’s curriculum committee meetings.

Course/program proposals are directed to the appropriate Senate Committee(s): undergraduate General Education courses to the General Education Committee (GEC); all other undergraduate courses/programs to the Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC); graduate courses/programs to the Graduate Council (GC).
These committees examine proposals with an eye to legibility and benefit to students. 5.
Full Senate Review.
The GEC, CASC, and the GC each make monthly reports to the entire Faculty Senate.
During these reports, they bring forward all new course/program proposals approved at the committee-level for a vote by the entire Senate.
Courses approved by this vote are then added to a bill for signature by the Faculty Senate President.
The President/Provost then provides final signature approval.
Concerns covered at this level typically include unexpected impacts on other programs or lack of resources.
Please note: 400 level courses proposed for graduate credit need to be approved by both the undergraduate and graduate committees within the department and college; at the Faculty Senate level, these proposals go before both the GC and CASC.

Please also note: courses are not approved for an immediate change; after completion of the approval process, they only become active in the term and year indicated in the proposal.
A complete proposal approved by each of the necessary levels might move through the process in 2-3 months.
Faculty submitting course proposals should carefully consult the meeting schedules for their college-level curriculum committee(s); the GEC, CASC, and GC; and the Faculty Senate itself.
They should also watch for notifications from Kuali if one of these bodies needs more information.

NEW CERTIFICATES, MINORS, or SPECIALIZATIONS COLLEGE OF EDUCATION: Minor in Global Education Studies, see Appendix H Global Education Studies (GES) minor allows students to explore globalization and internationalization of education and educational policies using the critical lens of equity and social justice, human rights and global citizenship.
The minor will prepare students with a diversity of backgrounds with the skill sets to become change agents and leaders in education in today’s globalized world.
This minor is part of the College of Education, as K-16 education are important components of the program.
However, students from all majors are welcome to participate or take courses in the minor.
Students interested in pursuing careers in and outside of the U.S. in the field of K-16 education, governmental and non-governmental organizations, international agencies, further their studies of international issues are especially encouraged to pursue this minor.
The curriculum is focused on expanding students’ knowledge, skills, and understanding of specific comparative and international theories, concepts, and practices in education.

The minor includes a requirement for participation in a faculty-led program in one of the College of Education’s study abroad programs in education or equivalent international experience such as COIL.
To declare a minor in Global Studies in Education a student must contact their major academic advisor at their College.
A program advisor at the College of Education will facilitate the students’ progress toward the minor and help assure that all requirements will be met for completion of the minor.
Minor Requirements: Global Education Studies (GES) minors must complete 18 or more credits related to global, comparative, and international education offered by different departments.
Requirements include a core of nine credits at the College of Education as follows: 1) EDC441-Comparative and International Education; 2) EDC330-Introduction to MLL Education; 3) Participation in a Faculty led study abroad program or an internship that is equivalent (i.e.
COIL (Collaborative Online International Learning, transfer course from another study abroad program).
We have a partnership with BridgeTEFL, students can transfer credits from this program, toward certification to teach English abroad.

Students will also choose a minimum of one language course from the Languages department or proficiency in another language that may not be offered in the languages department.
This can be waived for a student who has grown up in a multilingual household, or who has lived and studied at least three years or more in a foreign country including grades 1-12 (or equivalent).
For those students, these three credits can be replaced with electives.
Finally, students will take two electives from the approved courses.
Non-Education majors must also take EDC103 G in place of one of their electives.
Other international/global courses may be used as electives if approved by advisor.

This major is designed for undergraduate students who seek to expand their repertoire of writing for various publicprofessional and privatepublic audiences.
Graduates will have a strong foundation in rhetoricalWriting Studies theory balanced with a wide range of situational practices common to contemporary professional and public writers.
Coursework isincludes balanced between in-class learning, writing technology practice, peer and instructor feedback, and experiential �eldwork in real-world settings.
All graduates design their own digital electronic portfolios prior to graduation, demonstrating their ability to work with a range of technologies into producingproduce and distributingdistribute their polishedaudience- focused, effective writing.
WritingProfessional and rhetoricPublic Writing majors must complete 30 credits (maximum 51) including the core courses of WRT 201104, 235, 360371G, 404, and 495.

At least 15 credits for the major must be completed from writing courses numbered 300 or above.
WritingMajors and rhetoric majors are strongly encouraged to complete a practicum experience, such as an internship (WRT 477) or a �eld experience course (WRT 383 or 385).
A maximum of three credits for each of these experiential courses can count towards the major, unless the project substantially changes.
Undergraduates wishing to take a 500- or 600-level course must secure the instructor’s permission.
Students selecting this major may but are not required to pursue a concentration in either Technical Writing or Professional and Civic Writing.

To complete a concentration, students take nine credits from among the following: Technical Writing: WRT 306: Writing Health and Disability; WRT 332: Technical Writing; WRT 334: Science Writing; WRT 375: Human-Centered Design; WRT 477: Internship in Writing and Rhetoric; WRT 533: Seminar in Graduate Writing in the Life Sciences; WRT 534: Visualizing Environmental Advocacy Professional and Civic Writing: WRT 227: Business Communications (to be renamed Professional Writing); WRT 235: Digital Writing and Rhetoric; WRT 302: Writing Culture; WRT 303: Public Writing; WRT 305: Travel Writing; WRT 321G: Writing Disaster—the Ethics of Representation; WRT/PRS 331: Writing Public Relations; WRT 388: Proposal Writing for Clients; WRT 404: Writing with Community Partners.
The Harrington School of Communication and Media requires students in each of the six undergraduate majors to also complete the Harrington core requirements.
In order to transfer from University College for Academic Success to the College of Arts and Sciences as a Professional and Public Writing major, students must complete 24 credits and have a 2.00 GPA.
A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.
